lesson.title: Turning Names Into Numbers: Inside the Domain Name System
lesson.summary: DNS is the internet's hierarchical, distributed database that translates human readable domain names into IP addresses, using a tree of authoritative servers and a caching resolver system so that no single server has to know every name on the internet.
lesson.body:
The application layer protocols covered earlier, the ones users and their software actually interact with, are ultimately addressed at the network layer by IP addresses, but people, and most application configuration, work with names like www.example.com rather than something like 93.184.216.34. Something has to bridge that gap, reliably, at the scale of hundreds of millions of registered domain names, without requiring any single machine to hold the complete mapping from every name to every address. DNS is itself an application layer protocol, traditionally carried over UDP on port 53 for its typically small query and response messages, with a fallback to TCP for larger responses.

DNS solves this with a hierarchy that mirrors the dot-separated structure of a domain name, read in order of authority from right to left. At the top sits the root, then top level domains such as .com, .org, or country codes like .uk, then the domain itself, such as example.com, then any subdomains, such as www.example.com. Each level in this tree is served by authoritative name servers responsible only for their own narrow slice, called a zone. Root servers know only which servers are authoritative for each top level domain, nothing more. A .com TLD server knows only which servers are authoritative for example.com specifically, it never needs to know example.com's actual address records, and so on down the tree. This delegation of narrow responsibility is exactly what lets the whole system scale: correctness for any one domain rests entirely with whoever operates that domain's own authoritative server, not with the root or with any central authority.

An end host does not walk this tree itself. Its stub resolver simply asks a recursive resolver, typically operated by an ISP or by a public service, to do the work and hand back a final answer. The recursive resolver walks the hierarchy on the client's behalf, and critically, caches whatever answer it gets for a length of time set by that record's TTL, or time to live, value. This means the same or a related query can often be answered instantly from cache, with no repeat of the walk at all, which is the main reason DNS resolution feels fast in everyday use despite the layered hierarchy underneath it.

A full worked trace for a cold cache, resolving www.example.com, makes the whole process concrete. First, the stub resolver on a device asks its configured recursive resolver. Second, the recursive resolver has nothing relevant cached, so it asks a root server who is authoritative for .com. Third, the root server does not know example.com's address, but it does know which servers handle .com, and refers the resolver there. Fourth, the recursive resolver asks a .com TLD server about example.com specifically. Fifth, the TLD server does not know the actual address record either, but it does know which servers are authoritative for example.com, and refers the resolver there. Sixth, the recursive resolver asks that authoritative server directly for www.example.com. Seventh, the authoritative server, which actually holds the real records for that zone, returns the address record itself, for instance an IPv4 address such as 93.184.216.34. Eighth, the recursive resolver caches that answer for the duration of its TTL and finally returns it to the original stub resolver, which hands it to the application, now able to open a transport layer connection to that address. On every subsequent lookup for a popular domain, most of these steps are simply skipped, because some resolver along the chain already holds a cached, unexpired answer.

DNS also connects directly back to the RFC document prerequisite covered earlier. It is defined by two companion documents published in 1987, RFC 1034, which lays out the overall concepts and design, and RFC 1035, which specifies the actual wire format and protocol details. That makes DNS a clean, real world example of a foundational internet protocol whose entire behavior, down to individual record types and message formats, still traces directly back to a small number of specific, decades-old, and still current RFC documents.
